quests.instruction: A seedling has bright light and good soil, but nobody has given it a drink for a week, and it droops. Which need is missing?
quests.hint: Its roots have nothing left to take in.
quests.explanation: Plants need water to stay firm and to carry minerals from soil to leaves. When water runs out, stems and leaves go limp, or wilt.
quests.funFact: A wilted plant often perks up again within hours of being watered.

quests.instruction: Twenty seedlings are squeezed into one small pot, and all of them grow weak and thin. What is the most likely reason?
quests.hint: Think about twenty roots sharing the same small space.
quests.explanation: Crowded plants compete for light, water, and minerals, so none gets enough. Gardeners thin seedlings so the strongest can grow.
quests.funFact: Forest trees compete too, which is why they grow tall to reach the light.

quests.instruction: Leaves take in an invisible gas from the air to help make food. Which gas is it?
quests.hint: Animals breathe this gas out.
quests.explanation: Leaves take in carbon dioxide through tiny holes. Together with water and sunlight, it is turned into sugar.
quests.funFact: Animals breathe out the carbon dioxide that plants use.

quests.instruction: Which is the correct order for the life of a bean plant?
quests.hint: Everything begins with something tiny that is planted.
quests.explanation: A plant's life cycle goes from seed to seedling to adult plant. The adult makes flowers and new seeds, so the cycle begins again.
quests.funFact: A bean plant can make dozens of new seeds in one season.

quests.instruction: Which stage of a plant's life is the time when it makes seeds?
quests.hint: Seeds form where the flower once bloomed.
quests.explanation: After a flower is pollinated, it develops seeds. These seeds can grow into the next generation of plants.
quests.funFact: Some plants flower only once in their whole lives and then die.

quests.instruction: Which plant lives for hundreds of years, adding a new ring to its trunk each year?
quests.hint: The others finish their lives within a single season.
quests.explanation: Trees grow thicker each year and can live for hundreds of years. Many garden plants like beans and radishes live for only one growing season.
quests.funFact: Some oak trees have lived for more than 500 years.

quests.instruction: A bee moves from flower to flower with pollen stuck to its fuzzy body. What happens at the next flower?
options: The petals fall off at once 🌸
quests.hint: Think about why the bee ends up carrying it along.
quests.explanation: Pollen from one flower must reach another flower of the same kind so it can make seeds. This is called pollination.
quests.funFact: Many bees carry pollen in tiny baskets on their back legs.

quests.instruction: Which crop depends on wind, not bees, to carry its pollen?
quests.hint: Its flowers are small and make lots of dusty pollen.
quests.explanation: Wind-pollinated plants such as corn and grasses make huge amounts of light pollen. Apples and pumpkins rely on insects.
quests.funFact: A single corn plant can release millions of pollen grains.

quests.instruction: An orchard's apple blossoms are never visited by bees one spring. What will most likely happen?
quests.hint: Fruits form only after flowers are pollinated.
quests.explanation: Without pollination, most flowers cannot make fruit. This is why farmers value bees and sometimes keep hives near orchards.
quests.funFact: About a third of the food people eat depends on pollinators.

quests.instruction: As leaves make food, they release a gas that people and animals need to breathe. What is it?
quests.hint: You breathe it in right now.
quests.explanation: Plants release oxygen when they make food with sunlight. Animals, including people, need oxygen to live.
quests.funFact: Algae in the ocean also release much of the oxygen we breathe.

quests.instruction: Which everyday item is made from fibers found in wood?
quests.hint: Books are made from it.
quests.explanation: Wood is broken into fibers and pressed into sheets of paper. Recycling paper means fewer trees need to be cut.
quests.funFact: Most paper can be recycled several times.

quests.instruction: Along a tropical coast, tangled mangrove roots stand in the water. How do they help people living there?
quests.hint: Think about what a thick wall of roots does to rushing water.
quests.explanation: Mangrove roots slow waves and hold mud in place, protecting shores from erosion and giving fish nurseries.
quests.funFact: Mangrove roots are also nurseries for young fish and crabs.

quests.instruction: A plant in boggy soil snaps its leaves shut on flies to get extra nutrients. What is it?
quests.hint: Its hinged leaves close like jaws.
quests.explanation: Poor boggy soil lacks nutrients, so flytraps catch insects to get them. They still make most of their food from sunlight.
quests.funFact: A flytrap closes only if something touches its trigger hairs twice.

quests.instruction: Cactus roots spread out wide just under the soil. Why does that suit a desert?
quests.hint: Desert rain falls fast, then vanishes.
quests.explanation: Shallow, wide roots can soak up a brief shower before the water evaporates or sinks away.
quests.funFact: Some desert plants grow new roots within hours of rain.

quests.instruction: Plants on a dim rainforest floor often have very large leaves. What is the benefit?
quests.hint: Tall trees above them block most sunshine.
quests.explanation: Little sunlight reaches the forest floor, so big leaves help plants collect as much as possible.
quests.funFact: Only a small fraction of sunlight reaches the floor of some rainforests.

quests.instruction: A bean plant is 5 cm tall in week 2 and 9 cm tall in week 3. How much did it grow?
quests.hint: Subtract the smaller number from the larger.
quests.explanation: Comparing measurements over time shows how fast something grows. Growth often speeds up when plants get enough light and water.
quests.funFact: Bamboo can grow almost a meter in one day.

quests.instruction: Why do gardeners and scientists keep a plant journal with dates and drawings?
quests.hint: Think about what a single quick look cannot show you.
quests.explanation: Records let you compare how a plant looks now with how it looked before. That helps you see patterns, like growth spurts.
quests.funFact: Charles Darwin kept careful notebooks to study plants.

quests.instruction: A tiny green shoot has pushed up through a crack in a sidewalk. What made that possible?
quests.hint: Plants can be surprisingly strong.
quests.explanation: As roots and stems grow thicker, they push with real force. Over time they can widen cracks in pavement and rock.
quests.funFact: Tree roots can lift heavy sidewalk slabs.

quests.instruction: A fallen tree has 12 rings in its trunk. About how old was it?
quests.hint: Each ring marks a full round of seasons.
quests.explanation: In places with seasons, trees grow a new ring each year, so counting rings gives a tree's age.
quests.funFact: The oldest known living trees are over 4,000 years old.

quests.instruction: Some rings of a tree are thin and others are thick. What might a very thin ring tell us?
quests.hint: Growth slows when a tree is stressed.
quests.explanation: Trees grow less in years with little water, so those rings are narrow. Scientists read rings to learn about past weather.
quests.funFact: Tree rings have helped scientists study climate hundreds of years back.

quests.instruction: Trees in a dense forest often grow tall and straight. What is the benefit?
quests.hint: The leaves of neighboring trees block the light below.
quests.explanation: Tall growth lifts leaves above the shade of neighbors, so the tree can collect more sunlight.
quests.funFact: Young trees may grow upward fast when a nearby tree falls and opens the canopy.

quests.instruction: Why are plants called producers?
quests.hint: Think about who gets food from sunlight.
quests.explanation: Plants use sunlight to make food, so they are called producers. Most other living things depend on them.
quests.funFact: Almost every food chain starts with plants or similar producers.

quests.instruction: Thick plants grow along a riverbank. How do they help keep the river clean?
quests.hint: Think about what happens to loose soil in heavy rain.
quests.explanation: Roots hold soil in place and help trap dirt before it washes into the river. This keeps the water clearer for fish and plants.
quests.funFact: Wetland plants are sometimes called nature's filters.

quests.instruction: An old, hollow tree is home to owls, bats, and insects. What does this show about plants?
quests.hint: The tree is more than just food.
quests.explanation: Plants give animals places to nest, hide, and rest, as well as food. Even dead trees can shelter many animals.
quests.funFact: Fallen logs become homes for beetles, fungi, and salamanders.

quests.instruction: Cotton clothes are made from the soft fibers of which plant?
quests.hint: The fluffy fibers surround its seeds.
quests.explanation: The cotton plant grows fluffy fibers around its seeds. They are spun into thread and woven into cloth.
quests.funFact: One cotton plant can have many fluffy white bolls.

quests.instruction: Natural rubber is made from a milky sap collected from trees. Which item can be made from it?
quests.hint: Think of something that stretches and bounces.
quests.explanation: Sap from rubber trees is processed into rubber for boots, tires, and balls. Tapping the tree does not kill it.
quests.funFact: Rubber trees were first grown in the Amazon forest.

quests.instruction: Cinnamon is a spice used in cooking. Which part of the cinnamon tree is it?
quests.hint: It curls into little sticks when it dries.
quests.explanation: Cinnamon is the inner bark of a tree, peeled in thin layers and dried. Many spices come from different plant parts.
quests.funFact: Pepper is a seed, while ginger is an underground stem.

quests.instruction: Tomato seeds are planted, watered, and kept in a dark shed. What will probably happen?
quests.hint: Seeds can wake up in the dark, but then they need something else.
quests.explanation: Many seeds sprout without light, using stored food. Without sunlight, though, seedlings turn pale and weak because their leaves can't make food.
quests.funFact: Seedlings in the dark grow long and thin as they stretch for light.

quests.instruction: Which of these foods is actually a seed?
quests.hint: It grows inside a pod.
quests.explanation: Peas are seeds in a pod. Celery is mostly stem, and onions are swollen leaves around a bulb.
quests.funFact: Peas have been grown for thousands of years.

quests.instruction: A plant's leaves turn yellow and its soil is soaking wet and smells bad. What is the most likely problem?
quests.hint: Roots need air as well as water.
quests.explanation: Roots need air in the soil. If water fills all the gaps, roots can rot and the plant cannot take in what it needs.
quests.funFact: Pots with drainage holes help prevent overwatering.
